verPara: Separately from the status, we check whether each tool's npm or PyPI package links back to the listed repository.
title: Package audit: does the npm/PyPI package link back to the repo?
desc: We check whether each AI finance tool's npm or PyPI package links back to the repository we list. Live table, methodology and how to check yourself.
intro1: Many MCP servers and agent skills are installed with one line, like npx some-package or pip install some-package. That line pulls whatever is published under that name on npm or PyPI. That isn't always the code in the GitHub repository you just read.
intro2: Each week we check every tool in our directory: does the package named in the repo actually point back to that repo? This page shows the results.
latest: Latest check: {date}. Of {total} tools, {verified} have a package that links back to the listed repo. For {mm}, these are packages we couldn't link back to the listed repo. {none} have no npm or PyPI package. {norepo} are hosted APIs with no public repository.
note: A mismatch is not an accusation. Common harmless causes include a fork published under the original name, a repository that was renamed or moved, a separate wrapper package, or a package whose metadata simply leaves out the repository field. We report what we observed, not why it happened.

b.verified: The package named in the repo's package.json or pyproject.toml exists on npm or PyPI, and its metadata links back to the same GitHub repository.
b.mismatch: A package with that name exists, but its metadata points to a different repository.
b.unlinked: A package with that name exists, but its metadata has no repository link, so we couldn't link it back to this repo.
b.none: The repo doesn't declare a published npm or PyPI package at its root. Install from source as the README describes.

sep: These badges are separate from a tool's verification status (Verified, Aging, Stale…). A mismatch never changes that status.
m: For each listed repository, we read package.json at the repo root (skipping packages marked private) and pyproject.toml, and take the declared package name.
We look that name up on the public npm registry (registry.npmjs.org) or PyPI (pypi.org/pypi/<name>/json).

We check whether the package's metadata (npm: repository, homepage, bugs; PyPI: project_urls, home_page, download_url) contains the listed owner/repo. GitHub URLs are compared case-insensitively, after following GitHub's redirects for renamed or moved repositories.
We record the package name, latest version, its publish date and any repository the metadata declares.
notCheck: What we don't check: who controls the registry account, the contents of the published files, or install scripts. A "verified" badge means the links match. It doesn't mean the code was audited.
runs: The check runs weekly with the rest of our {verification}. Changes appear in the {weekly}. The data is available in {json} under CC BY 4.0 with attribution to TradingAIHub.
howH: How to check a package yourself
npm: Open https://www.npmjs.com/package/<name> and look at the "Repository" link in the sidebar. Does it match the repo you read?
Or run npm view <name> repository homepage maintainers.
Compare the latest version and publish date with the repo's releases or tags.
Before running npx, check for preinstall/postinstall scripts: npm view <name> scripts.
pypi: Compare the release history with the repo's tags.
either: If the metadata has no repository link, install from the repo's README instructions (for example npx github:owner/repo, pip install git+https://github.com/owner/repo, or a local clone).
Pin versions and prefer packages whose links match.
faq: Does "mismatch" mean a package is malicious?
No. It means the package's metadata doesn't link to the repository we list. Forks, renames, separate wrappers and missing metadata are the usual reasons.
Does "Package links back to repo" mean the code is safe?
No. It means the package and the repo link to each other. We don't audit code or install scripts.
Why do some tools show "No package"?
Many MCP servers are run from source or a container, and hosted APIs have no package. That's normal.
Weekly, together with our repository and endpoint checks. Changes appear in the weekly changelog.
I maintain one of these tools. How do I get the verified badge?

Add your repository URL to the package metadata (repository in package.json, or project_urls in pyproject.toml) and publish a new version. The next weekly run picks it up. You can also submit a correction.
